Issued at 250 AM CDT Sun Oct 25 2026

Early Sunday morning temperatures are running between 10-20 degrees 
cooler than 24-hours ago following Saturday's cold frontal passage. 
The front has stalled to the southeast of the forecast area and 
currently extends from central IA northeast into central WI. 
Locally, rain showers tied to a slow-moving moisture axis are 
expanding northeast out of southwestern MN and have reached the Twin 
Cities Metro. It's taken some time for the light precipitation to 
expand eastward due to the aforementioned PWAT/mid-level moisture 
axis serving as the driver of the shower chances (as opposed to the 
much more progressive surface front). Rain showers are forecast to 
linger through daybreak, eventually waning with time as the moisture 
axis slides south and drier air moves in. 

Cool and cloudy weather will be the theme to close the weekend, 
along with additional chances for light rain. Afternoon highs will 
struggle to warm out of the mid-50s for most locations. An upper-low 
currently spinning over the Four Corners region is forecast to lift 
north towards the Upper Midwest today into tomorrow. Mid-level warm 
advection will increase ahead of this feature, which will support 
the redevelopment of band of light precipitation across southern MN 
later this morning. The band is forecast to slowly lift north 
through the afternoon and evening in association with a northward 
shifting moisture axis. The highest PoPs are located across western 
MN, where forecast soundings depict greatest saturation. The upper-
low will pivot across the Great Plains tonight, spawning surface low 
pressure progged to track from central NE into northwestern MN. This 
will set the stage for a longer duration measurable rainfall event 
that will cover a good portion of the forecast area on Monday. 
Guidance illustrates the development of a broad precipitation shield 
ahead of the surface low, supported by isentropic ascent and PWATs 
200%+ of normal. Given the compact nature of this system, the 
regional swath of heaviest rainfall will be relatively narrow and 
highly track dependent. Fortunately, there has been little change in 
the overall placement of this zone across the guidance suite, as 
deterministic, global ensemble, and machine learning solutions are 
in fairly solid agreement that the axis of heaviest rainfall (1"-
1.5") will setup across eastern SD into far western MN. Rainfall 
amounts will lessen to the east of this swath, with corresponding 
amounts falling to a quarter to half inch or so from Mankato to the 
Twin Cities. Dry air flowing in from the southeast and displacement 
from the strongest forcing will limit amounts to a few hundredths 
across southeastern MN and most of western WI. The widespread rain 
will bring even cooler temperatures (40s) for Monday's highs. The 
precipitation shield will lift north of the forecast area by Tuesday 
morning.

A lull in the rain activity is forecast for much of the daytime 
hours Tuesday. However, the next shortwave in the active pattern is 
progged to advance east of the Rockies through the day. Associated 
surface low is forecast to translate northeast from the Dakotas into 
southern Canada, which places the Upper Midwest on the warm side of 
the system. Winds turn southerly on Tuesday and will combine with 
WAA to support highs climbing back into the mid 60s along and south 
of I-94 (perhaps near 70 along I-90). A warm front will lift through 
the region and spawn addition scattered shower chances later 
Tuesday. A few rumbles of thunder will also be possible. Mostly dry 
weather returns for Wednesday, though a few showers will be possible 
across the southeastern portion of the forecast area. Temperatures 
should remain quite mild in the 60s. 

There are two trends to highlight in the medium to extended forecast 
period (late week into the upcoming weekend): 1) The NBM is running 
warmer at the end of the work week, which follows the recent upward 
shift in ensemble guidance likely owing to large scale ridging. 
Could another 70 degree observation be in the cards for MSP prior to 
the end of October? Time will tell, but several members of ensemble 
suite suggest it is plausible on Friday! 2) There is a growing 
signal for wet weather next weekend across both global ensembles and 
machine learning counterparts. Unfortunately, the where and when is 
somewhat hard to decipher, but with western troughing set to follow 
the warm up, a system producing wet weather across the Upper Midwest 
is a possibility. The 40-60 PoPs from the NBM on Halloween may look 
a little spooky, but it is too early to lock into a wet forecast.
